entries.note: A full real run completed on 2026-09-13: 26 agents, 3,905 reasons, about 7 minutes, proving the pipeline end to end.
entries.reason: The plugin was released as v0.1.0 before any end-to-end run proved the full 3,905-reason pipeline works.

entries.note: A 3x3x3 smoke preset and subset dispatch make trial runs cheap instead of requiring the full 26-agent cost.
entries.reason: A full run costs 26 agent invocations and ~150k output tokens, discouraging casual trial runs.

entries.note: A smoke preset (3x3) gives the cheap trial run this reason says is missing.
entries.reason: The design fixes the tree at five-by-five across five levels with no smaller preview mode for trial runs.

entries.note: Complete trees are the user's stated requirement; the cheap-trial gap is handled by IMP-02 and IMP-01.
entries.reason: The author equated rigor with exhaustive breadth, assuming every node must be fully expanded.

entries.note: 5x5x5x5x5 is the user's explicit specification, not an unexamined reinterpretation; nothing further to change.
entries.reason: The Five Whys tradition was reinterpreted as five levels times five branches without questioning the multiplication.

entries.note: User research into preferred tree size is an organizational activity, not a plugin change.
entries.reason: No user research established what tree size people actually find useful.

entries.note: Past design emphasis; time-to-first-insight is now served by smoke preset and navigation (IMP-02, IMP-09).
entries.reason: Early design discussions focused on completeness claims rather than time-to-first-insight.

entries.note: Exhaustiveness is the user's requirement and remains the plugin's purpose; no artifact change follows.
entries.reason: Exhaustiveness was framed as the plugin's distinguishing feature versus simpler prompting.

entries.note: Author experience gap; the real run measured cost (1.2M tokens) and IMP-05 surfaces it to users.
entries.reason: The author lacked prior experience with how combinatorial fan-out explodes token budgets.

entries.note: BRANCHING and DEPTH are module constants; IMP-01 adds init --breadth/--depth stored in run.json.
entries.reason: Depth and fan-out are hard-coded constants in the script instead of configurable parameters.

entries.note: validate() uses the BRANCHING constant and a depth argument, not literal counts; parameterizing is IMP-01 plumbing.
entries.reason: The validator's shape checks were written against literal counts, making parameterization a larger refactor.

entries.note: Script prompts derive counts from constants, but SKILL.md and agent prose hard-code 5, 26 and 3,905; IMP-01 fixes.
entries.reason: The plan generator's prompts embed fixed counts like five reasons and 155 reasons as text.

entries.note: Shipping-speed motivation for v0.1.0; configuration itself is delivered by IMP-01.
entries.reason: Configuration was deferred to a later version to ship v0.1.0 faster.

entries.note: The script already uses argparse flags (--base, --depth, --id, --levels); init --breadth/--depth fit that convention.
entries.reason: The plugin scaffold had no settings file or CLI flag convention to hang options on.

entries.note: IMP-01 keeps each run uniform and complete while making the uniform shape configurable, preserving assembly simplicity.
entries.reason: Uniform shapes simplified the assembly code, so flexibility was traded for simplicity.

entries.note: A stdlib unittest suite exercises init, plan, check and assemble with synthetic fragments, no model calls.
entries.reason: No dry-run or stub mode exists to exercise orchestration without invoking real models.

entries.note: Tests generating placeholder fragments serve as the mock agent for pipeline coverage.
entries.reason: The script has no mock agent that emits placeholder fragments for pipeline testing.

entries.note: The claude plugin eval case runs the skill's prose orchestration end to end on a smoke preset.
entries.reason: Orchestration lives in skill prose executed by Claude, which cannot easily run offline.

entries.note: fivewhys.py already owns deterministic orchestration (plan, check, assemble); agents only generate fragment content.
entries.reason: Orchestration logic and content generation were not separated during design.

entries.note: claude plugin eval provides the dispatch harness; IMP-18 adds a smoke-preset eval case using it.
entries.reason: Plugin tooling offers no built-in harness for simulating sub-agent dispatch.

entries.note: There are still no tests in v0.1.0; IMP-11 adds the stdlib unittest suite.
entries.reason: Testing was treated as a post-release concern for an experimental first version.

entries.note: plan --only <id,...> dispatches chosen branches, giving on-demand single-branch expansion.
entries.reason: The skill offers no incremental mode that expands a single chosen branch on demand.

entries.note: plan emits root then all missing branches with no selection; --only lets users pick branch ids.
entries.reason: The plan command emits all 26 tasks at once rather than letting users select nodes.

entries.note: Partial state is tracked: per-branch fragment files persist and plan re-lists only missing or invalid ones.
entries.reason: Partial-tree state tracking was not designed into the run directory format.

entries.note: Complete trees stay the default, but --only permits branch-by-branch exploratory dispatch.
entries.reason: The UX assumed users want a finished tree, not an exploratory drill-down.

entries.note: assemble exits unless all 25 branches validate; assemble --partial writes a tree with missing-branch markers.
entries.reason: Assembly requires all 25 branch fragments present before producing any output.

entries.note: Selection lives in the script's plan --only flag, so the skill prose stays simple.
entries.reason: Interactive node selection would need more complex skill prompting than was budgeted.

entries.note: Splitting is also forced by output limits; the speed-versus-cost choice is past design, now measured by IMP-10.
entries.reason: The fan-out split into many branch agents was chosen for parallel speed rather than cost minimization.

entries.note: Prototyping pain point that motivated parallel dispatch; nothing further to change.
entries.reason: Wall-clock time was the most visible pain point during early prototyping.

entries.note: Past perception; the real run measured about 1.2M subagent tokens, and IMP-05 now surfaces cost.
entries.reason: Claude Code's parallel agent dispatch made splitting into many agents feel free.

entries.note: Per-run measurement in run.json and header quantifies agent overhead for future split decisions.
entries.reason: Per-agent overhead from system prompts and tool definitions was not measured when choosing the split.

entries.note: Model output-length limits are a platform fact that forces multiple agents regardless of plugin design.
entries.reason: Generating 3,905 reasons in one agent would exceed output limits, forcing some split anyway.

entries.note: Recorded tokens, duration and attempts per run supply the data a split-cost comparison needs.
entries.reason: No cost model compared 26 agents against fewer, larger-batched agents.

entries.note: 155 reasons per branch follows from 5x5 at three levels; configurable shape lets users choose smaller branches.
entries.reason: Each branch agent must emit 155 reasons as nested JSON, inflating output tokens.

entries.note: NEW reconciled: outline fragment format declined; real run's JSON fragments all passed first check.
entries.reason: Structural keys like reason and whys repeat thousands of times across the output.

entries.note: Validation-friendly format choice was reasonable; the token-economy remedy is the NEW outline format at 1.1.2.1.
entries.reason: The format was chosen for easy machine validation rather than token economy.

entries.note: NEW reconciled: plain-text fragment format declined; JSON validation stays exact.
entries.reason: No compact alternative such as indented plain text was evaluated before settling on JSON.

entries.note: Reliability rationale for JSON generation; any format change is proposed under 1.1.2.1.
entries.reason: Models produce JSON reliably, so it was the default to reduce parse failures.

entries.note: NEW reconciled: outline-to-JSON converter declined; generation format stays JSON.
entries.reason: The assembler expects nested objects, coupling generation format to storage format.

entries.note: Recording bytes and approximate tokens per run measures structural overhead that was never quantified.
entries.reason: Token cost of structural characters was never measured during design.

entries.note: Hygiene report flags over-length reasons without deleting; sentence length itself supports specificity.
entries.reason: Reasons are full sentences up to about 20 words rather than terse phrases.

entries.note: Readable specific causes are intended and reinforced by IMP-08; brevity is not a goal to change.
entries.reason: Agent instructions prioritize readable, specific causes over brevity.

entries.note: Sound rationale that terse phrases lose meaning for later analysis; no change implied.
entries.reason: Short phrases were judged too ambiguous for users analyzing the tree later.

entries.note: Average words per level recorded per run gives the baseline for any length calibration.
entries.reason: No experiment compared insight quality between eight-word and twenty-word reasons.

entries.note: Recorded average words and approximate tokens per level calibrate the limit against real budgets.
entries.reason: The word limit was picked intuitively rather than calibrated against a token budget.

entries.note: Justification for full-sentence reasons; it argues for keeping the current design.
entries.reason: Full sentences help readers understand deep nodes without scanning their ancestors.

entries.note: Isolated subagents need the problem and ancestor chain; this is small input cost, inherent to dispatch.
entries.reason: Every branch prompt restates the full problem description and ancestor chain.

entries.note: Claude Code subagents share no memory with each other; the plugin cannot change that.
entries.reason: Sub-agents share no memory, so context must be re-sent with every invocation.

entries.note: Problem length is the user's input for this run; the plugin uses statements verbatim by design.
entries.reason: The problem statement carries a long rating rationale that inflates every prompt.

entries.note: run.json already stores the problem; reading it from disk would cost the same input tokens anyway.
entries.reason: No shared context file lets agents read the problem once from disk.

entries.note: Isolated-agent clarity is the right priority; prompt restatement is a minor input cost.
entries.reason: Prompt templates were optimized for isolated-agent clarity, not total token spend.

entries.note: Per-subagent system prompt and tool definition loading is Claude Code platform behavior.
entries.reason: Each Claude Code sub-agent loads its own system prompt and tool definitions.

entries.note: Agent instructions gain targeted Edit repairs and a fix-loop cap instead of full rewrites.
entries.reason: Agents may need several write-and-check cycles, re-emitting the whole fragment each time.

entries.note: The agent says single Write of the whole fragment; IMP-08 replaces that with targeted Edit repairs.
entries.reason: Instructions require one Write of the whole file, so fixes tend to rewrite everything.

entries.note: check already reports path-located errors like whys[2].whys[4]: expected 5 reasons, got 4.
entries.reason: The checker reports errors without a patch-friendly location format.

entries.note: Outline-before-write instruction helps agents keep exactly five items across 155 nodes.
entries.reason: Keeping exactly five items across 155 nodes is error-prone for language models.

entries.note: No Edit repair path exists and the agent lacks the Edit tool; IMP-08 adds targeted repairs.
entries.reason: No Edit-based targeted repair path is suggested in the agent instructions.

entries.note: Losing nesting depth in long JSON is a model limitation; outline-before-write (IMP-08) mitigates it.
entries.reason: Models lose track of nesting depth in long generated JSON documents.

entries.note: 3,905 is intrinsic to complete 5x5 trees; configurable breadth and depth let users pick smaller complete trees.
entries.reason: The 3,905-reason total is intrinsic to a complete five-way tree five levels deep.

entries.note: Pruning geometric growth drops complete trees, which the user specified; shape is configurable instead.
entries.reason: Geometric growth of five to the nth power was accepted without a pruning strategy.

entries.note: Skipping low-value nodes yields incomplete trees and requires value judgment, both declined.
entries.reason: No mechanism skips low-value nodes that do not merit further expansion.

entries.note: A relevance filter is plugin-side pruning and judgment; analysis stays with the user.
entries.reason: The plugin lacks a relevance filter to stop expanding redundant or trivial causes.

entries.note: Variable fan-out or not-applicable slots break the required complete tree shape.
entries.reason: Fixed fan-out ignores that some causes naturally have fewer than five sub-causes.

entries.note: Adaptive depth is explicitly declined; every tree stays complete at the configured depth.
entries.reason: Depth is uniform instead of adapting to where root causes are actually found.

entries.note: init --model records a chosen model and the skill passes it as the Agent override.
entries.reason: Model inheritance runs all 26 agents on whatever expensive model the user's session uses.

entries.note: model: inherit remains default, but per-run model selection lets users pick cheaper models.
entries.reason: The agent definition specifies model inherit instead of pinning a cheaper model.

entries.note: Past assumption about quality needs; IMP-04 documents the model trade-off for users to decide.
entries.reason: The author assumed stronger models were needed to avoid repetitive, shallow causes.

entries.note: The unrevisited scaffold default is addressed by an explicit per-run model option.
entries.reason: Inherit was the scaffold default and was never revisited before release.

entries.note: IMP-04 docs explain the quality-cost trade-off; users choose rather than the plugin pinning blindly.
entries.reason: No quality comparison between Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus outputs was performed.

entries.note: IMP-04 uses stable aliases (inherit, sonnet, opus, haiku), avoiding breakage from versioned identifiers.
entries.reason: Pinning a model name risks breakage when model identifiers change.

entries.note: Keeping inherit as default with optional override accommodates differing plan access.
entries.reason: Users on different plans have different model access, making a fixed choice awkward.

entries.note: Model choice at invocation is exactly init --model plus the skill's Agent model override.
entries.reason: The skill offers no model or budget choice at invocation time.

entries.note: Skill argument handling gains a model option recorded in run.json.
entries.reason: The skill's argument handling only accepts the problem statement.

entries.note: plan emits the model per task and the skill passes it as the Agent model override.
entries.reason: Per-dispatch model overrides were not surfaced in the orchestration instructions.

entries.note: Past oversight; cost-sensitive users are served by IMP-02, IMP-04 and IMP-05.
entries.reason: The author did not anticipate cost-sensitive users trialing the plugin.

entries.note: Minimal-interface motivation for v0.1.0; options arrive via IMP-01, IMP-02 and IMP-04.
entries.reason: Options were deferred to keep the first release's interface minimal.

entries.note: Thin plugin configuration documentation is a Claude Code ecosystem fact.
entries.reason: Plugin conventions for user-facing configuration are thinly documented.

entries.note: Users' default session model choice is outside the plugin's control.
entries.reason: Power users commonly run Claude Code sessions on Opus with large context windows.

entries.note: Explicit per-run model selection and docs remind users subagents otherwise inherit Opus.
entries.reason: Users set Opus as default for coding quality and forget sub-agents inherit it.

entries.note: Claude Code lacks estimates, so init and plan report measured token estimates and confirm before dispatch.
entries.reason: Claude Code shows no per-sub-agent cost estimate before dispatch.

entries.note: Subscription plans hiding marginal cost is an Anthropic product fact, not plugin-controlled.
entries.reason: Subscription plans obscure marginal costs until rate limits are hit.

entries.note: Long-context variant usage pressure is a platform pricing and quota fact.
entries.reason: Long-context variants add usage pressure during extended sessions.

entries.note: A per-run model override removes the need to switch the session model.
entries.reason: Users rarely switch models mid-session just to run one plugin.

entries.note: README documents measured cost and time; README currently only says the file is about 150k tokens.
entries.reason: Cost information is absent from the plugin's documentation and launch messages.

entries.note: A full run on 2026-09-13 measured about 1.2M subagent tokens, 26 agents, about 7 minutes.
entries.reason: The author had not measured a real full run's token usage to report.

entries.note: README gains measured cost, time, limitations and concurrency cap sections.
entries.reason: README content focused on how the method works, not what it costs.

entries.note: run.json and header record size, tokens, duration and attempts; a telemetry backend is declined (R-05).
entries.reason: No telemetry captures per-run token counts for later documentation.

entries.note: Psychological reluctance to disclose cost; disclosure is now planned in IMP-14.
entries.reason: Cost disclosures feel discouraging, so early releases tend to omit them.

entries.note: The skill confirms with the user, showing agent and token estimates, before a full-size run.
entries.reason: The skill does not show a confirmation step summarizing expected spend.

entries.note: Preview and confirmation show usage impact before dispatching 26 agents against subscription limits.
entries.reason: Subscription rate limits make 26 parallel agents consume a large share of usage.

entries.note: Plan-level dispatch waves bounded by a configurable cap shape the burst instead of ad hoc batches.
entries.reason: Parallel dispatch concentrates usage into a short burst that hits throttling windows.

entries.note: Quota sharing across a user's Claude work is a subscription platform fact.
entries.reason: Usage quotas are shared with the user's other ongoing coding work.

entries.note: Wave size is configurable below the default 20, allowing a throttled dispatch pace.

entries.note: Remaining quota visibility is a Claude Code/subscription feature the plugin cannot provide.
entries.reason: Users cannot see remaining quota before deciding to launch a run.

entries.note: Measured output is about 128k tokens; show, index.md and branch-by-branch loading allow partial reading.
entries.reason: The assembled output is meant to be read into context whole, adding another ~150k tokens.

entries.note: A summarization or synthesis layer is plugin-side interpretation, declined per the user's requirement.

entries.note: Deliberate, still-valid motivation matching the requirement that analysis belongs to the user.
entries.reason: The author wanted to avoid AI-imposed interpretations biasing root-cause conclusions.

entries.note: Synthesis is declined on principle, not difficulty; mechanical aids (IMP-06, IMP-09) substitute.

entries.note: This risk is exactly why plugin-side ranking stays declined.

entries.note: The raw tree as product is the user's requirement; no change implied.
entries.reason: The design treats the raw tree as the product rather than as an intermediate.

entries.note: How rate-limit errors surface to sub-agents and parents is Claude Code behavior.
entries.reason: Rate-limit hits in sub-agents surface as vague failures rather than explicit quota messages.

entries.note: Error code propagation from agents to parent is controlled by the platform.
entries.reason: Agent failures reach the parent without underlying API error codes.

entries.note: Throttling manifesting as slowness is service behavior outside the plugin.
entries.reason: A throttled agent may simply run slower, hiding the cause entirely.

entries.note: Automatic client retries are implemented by Claude Code, not the plugin.
entries.reason: Automatic client retries mask how often limits are actually hit.

entries.note: Orchestrator visibility into timeout versus rate-limit causes is a platform limitation.
entries.reason: Timeouts and rate limits look identical from the orchestrator's perspective.

entries.note: The reply already carries FAILED with first error; IMP-12 formalizes failure semantics and stuck reporting.
entries.reason: The one-line reply format has no field for reporting error types.

entries.note: Waves sized to a configurable concurrency cap (default 20) let users on different tiers pace runs.
entries.reason: Plugin users span many plan tiers, so no single safe concurrency level exists.

entries.note: Throughput differences across plan tiers are provider facts.
entries.reason: Pro, Max, team, and API-key users have very different throughput ceilings.

entries.note: Claude Code exposes no tier detection to plugins.
entries.reason: The plugin cannot detect which tier the current user is on.

entries.note: A configurable wave size avoids hard-coding the lowest-tier pace for everyone.
entries.reason: Designing for the lowest tier would make runs painfully slow for heavy users.

entries.note: No quota or capacity API exists to probe; fixed configurable waves (IMP-03) are the feasible substitute.
entries.reason: No adaptive strategy probes available capacity and adjusts concurrency accordingly.

entries.note: Studying users' environments is user research, out of scope for plugin changes.
entries.reason: Marketplace distribution means the author never sees most users' environments.

entries.note: The smoke preset gives cheap rehearsal runs instead of spending quota on full attempts.
entries.reason: Discovering limits empirically would itself burn significant quota.

entries.note: A 3x3 smoke preset and plan --only subset dispatch avoid consuming a full window per attempt.
entries.reason: Each full attempt consumes a large share of a usage window.

entries.note: Partial assembly turns interrupted attempts into usable output; valid fragments already persist for resume.
entries.reason: Failed attempts yield little reusable output, discouraging repeated experiments.

entries.note: Smoke preset and subset dispatch provide a cheap stand-in for rehearsing orchestration.
entries.reason: No mock agent or cheap stand-in exists to rehearse orchestration without real generation.

entries.note: Personal budget psychology; cheap rehearsal is covered by IMP-02.
entries.reason: Personal budget pressure makes speculative heavy runs feel wasteful.

entries.note: Author's competing daily usage explains past caution; nothing further in the plugin.
entries.reason: Quota spent on testing competes with the author's other daily Claude Code work.

entries.note: Plan-emitted waves move pacing from prose instructions into deterministic script output.
entries.reason: Orchestration lives in natural-language skill instructions, which cannot enforce pacing reliably.

entries.note: Pre-grouped waves from plan leave the model no batching decision to reinterpret.
entries.reason: Models may ignore or reinterpret instructions about batching and waiting between dispatches.

entries.note: Runtime tool-call grouping being model-decided is how Claude Code agents work.
entries.reason: Prompts express intent, but the model decides tool-call grouping at runtime.

entries.note: Encoding waves in plan output replaces reliance on one rule's salience in the 86-line skill.
entries.reason: Long skill instructions dilute the salience of any single operational rule.

entries.note: Instruction-following differences across model versions are outside plugin control.
entries.reason: Model versions differ in how literally they follow dispatch guidance.

entries.note: An eval running a smoke-preset run end to end exercises actual orchestrator dispatch.
entries.reason: No deterministic harness verifies the orchestrator's actual dispatch behavior.

entries.note: Claude Code's system guidance favoring concurrent agents is a platform fact.
entries.reason: General system guidance favors launching independent agents concurrently.

entries.note: Scripts cannot spawn Claude Code sub-agents; that is a platform constraint.
entries.reason: The Python script cannot launch sub-agents, so dispatch control cannot move into code.

entries.note: Agent spawning exposed only as a model tool is Claude Code's design.
entries.reason: Claude Code exposes agent spawning as a model tool, not a scriptable plugin API.

entries.note: Driving the Agent SDK from the script needs API keys and network calls, which the catalog declines.
entries.reason: Using the Agent SDK directly would move the plugin outside the plugin model.

entries.note: Headless CLI dispatch from the script adds network-calling model runs to a stdlib offline script; declined.
entries.reason: Headless CLI invocation from the script was not considered for dispatch.

entries.note: Deliberate single-session simplicity choice; still the intended design.
entries.reason: Keeping everything inside one session was a deliberate simplicity choice.

entries.note: Author unfamiliarity explanation; pacing is covered by plan waves in IMP-03.
entries.reason: Workflow scripting features that could pace agents were new or unfamiliar to the author.

entries.note: plan checks fragments on disk each round and assemble validates all, independent of the model reading replies.
entries.reason: Failure handling depends on the orchestrating model noticing and reacting to each result.

entries.note: The model need not track results: plan re-derives remaining tasks from files every round.
entries.reason: Twenty-five results arriving asynchronously strain the model's bookkeeping.

entries.note: FAILED replies and attempt counts get explicit semantics: record attempts, report tasks stuck past 3.
entries.reason: FAILED replies are not mapped to a specific retry action in the skill.

entries.note: assemble validates every fragment and refuses to write output if any is missing or invalid.
entries.reason: The model may proceed to assembly without confirming every fragment passed.

entries.note: The skill's three-round rule becomes per-task attempt counts recorded by the script.
entries.reason: Retry counts and limits per branch are undefined, so reactions vary by run.

entries.note: Failure semantics (attempts, stuck tasks, capped fix loops) extend handling beyond the happy path.
entries.reason: Error handling instructions were written for the happy path first.

entries.note: plan will group tasks into waves no larger than the concurrency cap.
entries.reason: The plan output hands over all 25 branch prompts at once, nudging simultaneous dispatch.

entries.note: Directly the missing wave grouping in plan output.
entries.reason: The plan command emits a single flat task list without wave or batch grouping.

entries.note: Past schema simplicity choice; wave grouping is IMP-03.
entries.reason: A flat list is the simplest schema for the script to generate and consume.

entries.note: Pacing becomes an explicit design goal through wave metadata in plan.
entries.reason: Wave metadata was omitted because dispatch pacing was never a design goal.

entries.note: How models interpret task lists is model behavior; IMP-03 structures the list instead.
entries.reason: Models read a list of independent tasks as a signal for maximal parallelism.

entries.note: Waves subdivide the branch phase into cap-sized groups.
entries.reason: Root and branch phases were separated, but branches were never subdivided further.

entries.note: A plugin eval exercising a smoke-preset run makes orchestration behavior testable before real runs.
entries.reason: Prompt-based orchestration is hard to test, so pacing problems stay hidden until real runs.

entries.note: Unit tests will cover waves, failure attempts and partial assembly paths without live agents.
entries.reason: No eval suite simulates slow, failing, or throttled sub-agents.

entries.note: Adds an evals/ case for claude plugin eval.
entries.reason: Plugin eval tooling has not been adopted for this plugin.

entries.note: Model nondeterminism is outside plugin control; live-model CI is declined under R-05.
entries.reason: Nondeterministic model behavior makes orchestration tests flaky and expensive.

entries.note: Agent tool mockability is a Claude Code limitation.
entries.reason: The Agent tool cannot easily be mocked inside normal Claude Code sessions.

entries.note: v0.1.0 has no tests at all, even for the validator; IMP-11 adds them.
entries.reason: Testing effort went to the deterministic Python validator instead.

entries.note: A non-blocking hygiene report flags duplicates, near-duplicates, parent restatements and over-length reasons beyond shape validation.
entries.reason: Validation checks only JSON shape, so vacuous, off-topic, or duplicated reasons pass as valid output.

entries.note: The implied model-based judge in the check loop is declined as flaky and costly; stdlib hygiene flags substitute.
entries.reason: Structure checks are deterministic Python, while judging reason quality requires semantic, model-based evaluation.

entries.note: Shape-only validation as the whole goal is extended by assemble's hygiene report covering duplicates, restatements and over-length reasons.
entries.reason: The author built the validator first to guarantee assembly works, treating shape correctness as the minimum viable goal.

entries.note: Shape failures blocking all output is softened by partial assembly with explicit missing-branch markers.
entries.reason: Assembly breaks outright on malformed fragments, making shape failures the most visible and urgent risk.

entries.note: Malformed model JSON is model behaviour; the existing check already catches it and agents repair before assembly.
entries.reason: JSON from language models often has trailing text, wrong nesting, or miscounted lists.

entries.note: assemble validates every fragment first and exits with a re-dispatch message; it does not crash, though it refuses partial output.
entries.reason: The assembler walks fixed-depth lists and crashes on any missing or extra item.

entries.note: Speculation about early prototype parse errors; nothing further actionable beyond the existing check.
entries.reason: Early prototype runs likely hit parse errors before any content could be inspected.

entries.note: One bad fragment blocking the whole run is addressed by assemble --partial producing a valid tree with missing markers.
entries.reason: A crash blocks the whole run, while a weak reason silently degrades only one node.

entries.note: Silent quality failures get surfaced as non-blocking hygiene flags written to hygiene.json at assembly.
entries.reason: Silent quality failures generate no error messages, so nothing prompts the author to act on them.

entries.note: Scoping v0.1.0 as pipeline proof explains history; quality follow-ups are tracked by other catalog codes.
entries.reason: Version 0.1.0 was scoped as a proof of pipeline, not a finished quality product.

entries.note: Prioritizing fan-out mechanics first is past motivation; refinement now proceeds through the catalog improvements.
entries.reason: The author wanted working fan-out mechanics before investing in refinement features.

entries.note: Solo developer time pressure explains deferral; no artifact change follows from it.
entries.reason: Solo plugin development offers limited time, pushing polish into later versions.

entries.note: Lack of early users explains past priorities; the plugin is now public, and recruiting feedback is out of scope.
entries.reason: No users or feedback existed yet to demand quality guarantees.

entries.note: Ship-early norms in plugin ecosystems are industry culture the plugin cannot change.
entries.reason: Shipping early is the norm in plugin ecosystems where iteration is cheap.

entries.note: Untracked deferral is remedied by the self-improvement tree, catalog and ledger recording each change and its reason.
entries.reason: Quality validation was implicitly deferred without a tracked roadmap item.

entries.note: Deterministic checks fitting a short window explains how v0.1.0 came to be; nothing further to change.
entries.reason: Deterministic checks are fast to write and verify, fitting a short development window.

entries.note: True that shape checks are small stdlib code; this explains the choice without implying a change.
entries.reason: Counting list lengths and keys takes a few dozen lines of standard-library Python.

entries.note: A fully specified schema made shape checking the easy first step; past design rationale only.
entries.reason: Shape rules are fully specified by the 5x5 schema, leaving no design decisions open.

entries.note: Hand-testing the checker with malformed files is replaced by a stdlib unittest suite covering check and assemble.
entries.reason: The checker can be tested by hand with a few malformed files in minutes.

entries.note: Calibrated semantic model checks are declined; stdlib hygiene heuristics substitute without prompt design or example sets.
entries.reason: Semantic checks would require prompt design, calibration, and example sets the author lacked.

entries.note: Developer preference for finishable work is general psychology behind v0.1.0; nothing actionable remains.
entries.reason: Developers default to work they can finish and see pass in one sitting.

entries.note: Relying on prompts alone is backed by a downstream mechanical hygiene layer flagging duplicates and restatements.
entries.reason: The design assumed sub-agent prompts alone would produce adequate reasons.

entries.note: Distinctness and no-restatement rules gain mechanical detection via hygiene flags, closing the enforcement gap without blocking.
entries.reason: Agent instructions already state distinctness and causal rules, creating a false sense of enforcement.

entries.note: Failure rates hidden by short tests become visible as hygiene counts over full-scale assembled trees.
entries.reason: Strong models usually follow instructions well in short tests, masking failure rates at scale.

entries.note: A full real 3,905-reason run completed on 2026-09-13 with 26 agents.
entries.reason: No full 3,905-reason run was done to reveal where instructions are ignored.

entries.note: Prompt authors overestimating compliance is a general industry tendency outside plugin control.
entries.reason: Prompt authors often overestimate instruction compliance across hundreds of parallel generations.

entries.note: Past trust in the model explains the missing layer; the verification need is covered by IMP-06.
entries.reason: Trust in the model reduced the perceived need for a downstream verification layer.

entries.note: The user-analysis stance is clarified to allow mechanical quality aids while interpretation stays with the user.
entries.reason: Analysis was deliberately left to the user, and that stance extended to judging reason quality.

entries.note: Generator-not-evaluator framing is kept but documented to permit hygiene flags, navigation and measurement.
entries.reason: The plugin's philosophy frames itself as a generator, not an evaluator.

entries.note: Automated filtering or pruning stays declined; hygiene flags annotate only and delete nothing.
entries.reason: The author worried automated filtering would bias or prune reasons the user wanted to see.

entries.note: Hygiene flags define concrete mechanical standards inside the tool without making quality judgments for the user.
entries.reason: Treating the user as final reviewer avoided defining quality standards inside the tool.

entries.note: Short focused agent prompts are a past design rationale; nothing actionable follows.
entries.reason: Separating generation from judgment kept the agent prompts short and focused.

entries.note: Reviewing 3,905 reasons by hand is eased by show, index.md of levels 1-2 and branch-by-branch loading guidance.
entries.reason: No one tested whether users can realistically review 3,905 reasons by hand.

entries.note: Model calls, API keys and network access from the script are declined to keep the offline zero-dependency install.
entries.reason: Calling a model from the script would need API keys, network access, and costs the plugin avoids.

entries.note: Plugin scripts lacking access to the session's model connection is a Claude Code architecture fact.
entries.reason: Plugin scripts run as local subprocesses without access to the session's authenticated model connection.

entries.note: Claude Code not exposing its model session to Bash scripts is platform behaviour.
entries.reason: Claude Code does not expose its model session to Bash-invoked scripts.

entries.note: CLI credential handling and isolation from child processes is controlled by Claude Code, not the plugin.
entries.reason: Credentials are managed by the CLI and intentionally not passed to child processes.

entries.note: Absence of a plugin completion API for scripts is a platform limitation.
entries.reason: No documented plugin API lets scripts request completions from the host.

entries.note: Subscription users lacking standalone API keys is an Anthropic account-model fact.
entries.reason: Subscription-based users may have no standalone API key at all.

entries.note: Subprocess isolation from privileged host capabilities is Claude Code's security design.
entries.reason: Security design isolates tool subprocesses from privileged host capabilities.

entries.note: Requiring an API key is declined; the plugin stays usable immediately after install.
entries.reason: Requiring a separate API key would add setup friction that discourages plugin adoption.

entries.note: Marketplace expectations of zero-configuration plugins are ecosystem norms.
entries.reason: Marketplace plugins are expected to work immediately after install with no configuration.

entries.note: Console accounts and billing separate from subscriptions are Anthropic product facts.
entries.reason: Users would need a Console account and billing separate from their subscription.

entries.note: Environment-variable key setup is avoided entirely because API keys in the script are declined.
entries.reason: Environment-variable setup errors produce confusing failures new users struggle to debug.

entries.note: Install-time friction losing casual users is general adoption behaviour outside plugin control.
entries.reason: Friction at install time loses most casual users before their first run.

entries.note: Shareability without key documentation remains a deliberate constraint; key-based features stay declined.
entries.reason: The author wanted the plugin shareable without documentation about keys.

entries.note: An API-based review pass over all reasons is declined; stdlib hygiene checks cost no tokens.
entries.reason: Reviewing 3,905 reasons via API would add substantial token cost on top of generation.

entries.note: Per-reason model judging with repeated ancestor context is declined for cost; mechanical flags replace it.
entries.reason: Judging each reason in context requires resending the problem and ancestor chain repeatedly.

entries.note: Duplicate detection uses stdlib token overlap in hygiene.json, avoiding embeddings and pairwise model comparisons.
entries.reason: Duplication checks compare reasons pairwise or by embedding, scaling badly across thousands of items.

entries.note: Generation cost at default-model prices is addressed by init --model letting users choose a cheaper tier.
entries.reason: Generation already consumes 26 sub-agent contexts at default-model prices.

entries.note: Doubled cost from a model quality pass is avoided because model judging is declined in favour of free flags.
entries.reason: Users paying per token would see roughly doubled costs for a quality pass.

entries.note: Model tier selection becomes explicit via init --model recorded in run.json, with documented trade-offs.
entries.reason: No cheap model tier was selected or benchmarked for evaluation work.

entries.note: Network-dependent validation is declined; check stays a fast offline stdlib call.
entries.reason: Network-dependent validation would make the check command slow and failure-prone.

entries.note: Latency multiplied by fix-loop retries is avoided because no model judge runs inside the blocking loop.
entries.reason: Sub-agents run the check in a fix loop, so latency multiplies across retries.

entries.note: Rate-limited check calls cannot occur because the script makes no network calls.
entries.reason: Rate limits during 26 parallel agents would cause check calls to fail.

entries.note: Offline environments keep working because network calls in the script are declined.
entries.reason: Offline or restricted network environments would break validation entirely.

entries.note: Timeout retry logic is unnecessary since the script stays network-free.
entries.reason: Timeouts would need retry logic the simple script does not have.

entries.note: Infrastructure failures muddling content errors is avoided by keeping model judgment out of the blocking check.
entries.reason: A check that fails for infrastructure reasons muddles genuine content errors.

entries.note: The stdlib-only choice is kept and documented in the README's design decisions section.
entries.reason: Standard-library-only Python was chosen to avoid dependency installation.

entries.note: Plugins lacking a pip install mechanism is a Claude Code platform fact.
entries.reason: Plugins have no built-in mechanism to install pip packages on the user's machine.

entries.note: Anthropic SDK or embedding libraries requiring virtual environments are declined third-party dependencies.
entries.reason: The Anthropic SDK or embedding libraries would require virtual environments and version management.

entries.note: Python version variety across user machines is environmental; stdlib-only already sidesteps package brittleness.
entries.reason: Varied Python versions across user machines make third-party packages brittle.

entries.note: Preference for one portable script is past rationale; its documentation is covered by IMP-14.
entries.reason: The author prioritized a single portable script that runs anywhere python3 exists.

entries.note: Auditability of dependency-free scripts supports the declined third-party packages disposition.
entries.reason: Dependency-free scripts are easier to audit for a plugin marketplace.

entries.note: The concrete, encodable subset of quality (duplicates, restatements, length) gets coded as hygiene flags.
entries.reason: No rubric defines what makes a reason good, so there is nothing concrete to encode in code.

entries.note: Subjective, context-dependent quality judgments are explicitly assigned to the user, separate from mechanical aids.
entries.reason: Reason quality in Five Whys is inherently subjective and context-dependent.

entries.note: Missing domain knowledge is reduced by optional context intake stored in run.json and included in every prompt.
entries.reason: Whether a cause is plausible depends on domain knowledge the tool does not have.

entries.note: Differing user values for breadth, depth or actionability are left to user interpretation by stated principle.
entries.reason: Different users value breadth, depth, or actionability differently.

entries.note: Brief problem statements trigger one clarifying ask for key specifics, stored and passed to all agents.
entries.reason: The problem statement is often brief, leaving the true context unknown.

entries.note: Practitioner disagreement on root-cause definitions is a methodology-field fact outside plugin control.
entries.reason: Five Whys practitioners themselves disagree on what counts as a root cause.

entries.note: Subjectivity is accommodated with non-blocking flags instead of hard pass-fail quality criteria.
entries.reason: Subjectivity discourages writing hard pass-fail criteria.

entries.note: The self-run tree and 3,905-entry disposition ledger form a labeled example set kept in docs/self-improvement.
entries.reason: The author has not collected example runs labeled good or bad to derive criteria from.

entries.note: A full real run completed on 2026-09-13 and is stored as docs/self-improvement/tree.json.
entries.reason: No full real run exists to supply material for labeling.

entries.note: Tedious labeling is being done once as the self-improvement ledger, retained as dogfooding evidence.
entries.reason: Labeling hundreds of reasons is tedious work with no immediate payoff.

entries.note: An evals/ case for claude plugin eval adds the missing eval harness.
entries.reason: There is no eval harness in the repository to store examples.

entries.note: Recruiting a second reviewer for label agreement is an organizational remedy, not a plugin change.
entries.reason: The project lacks a second reviewer to establish agreement on labels.

entries.note: Observed failures are now gathered: the full run's tree and this catalog record them.
entries.reason: Criteria usually emerge from observed failures, which have not been gathered yet.

entries.note: Distinctness and restatement are operationalized mechanically; causality and specificity stay with the user.
entries.reason: Quality dimensions like causality, distinctness, and specificity are hard to operationalize individually.

entries.note: Causality cannot be string-checked, so it is explicitly left to user interpretation rather than faked.
entries.reason: Causal relationships cannot be verified by string features or keywords.

entries.note: Uncalibrated similarity thresholds are tolerable because near-duplicate flags only annotate and never block.
entries.reason: Distinctness needs semantic similarity thresholds that are arbitrary without calibration.

entries.note: Per-level word averages recorded in the output expose specificity variation without imposing one threshold.
entries.reason: Specificity legitimately varies by level, so any single threshold is wrong at some depths.

entries.note: Interacting judgments like specific-yet-not-causal remain the user's; the tool flags only mechanical issues.
entries.reason: Dimensions interact, so a reason can be specific yet not causal.

entries.note: Scarcity of published automatic root-cause scoring methods is a research-field fact.
entries.reason: Published methods for automatically scoring root cause reasoning are sparse.

entries.note: Agent instructions gain concrete grounding, stated assumptions and specific-vs-generic examples instead of loose style guidance.
entries.reason: The agent instructions describe style guidance rather than measurable acceptance criteria.

entries.note: Vague words like plausible and concrete get anchored by a specific-vs-generic example in the agent instructions.
entries.reason: Words like plausible and concrete were written for a model reader, not a checker.

entries.note: hygiene.json provides a structured, checkable counterpart to the prose quality guidance.
entries.reason: Instructions were authored as prose markdown with no structured quality schema.

entries.note: check enforces item counts, non-empty reasons and leaf shape only; the 20-word guidance is not encoded anywhere.
entries.reason: The only numeric rules are item counts and word length, which is what got encoded.

entries.note: Prose feeling sufficient for a model reader explains v0.1.0; specifics are covered by IMP-08.
entries.reason: Prose guidance feels sufficient when the reader is another model.

entries.note: The eval suite grades smoke runs for shape and hygiene report presence, turning guidance into testable assertions.
entries.reason: No development step translated the guidance into testable assertions.

entries.note: Lean-practice origin of the method is background history with nothing further to change.
entries.reason: The method was adopted from lean practice, where quality is judged in facilitated human sessions.

entries.note: Traditional facilitator-led Five Whys is a methodology fact outside the plugin.
entries.reason: Traditional Five Whys relies on a facilitator challenging weak answers live.

entries.note: Lean training materials lacking automated scoring is an external ecosystem fact.
entries.reason: Lean training materials describe good practice, not automated scoring.

entries.note: An automated facilitator challenging answers would be a model judge in the loop, which is declined.
entries.reason: Translating a group method into an automated pipeline dropped the facilitator role.

entries.note: No manual precedent for 3,905-reason fan-outs is a methodology-field fact.
entries.reason: A 3,905-reason fan-out has no precedent in manual practice to borrow standards from.

entries.note: Social quality controls like facilitators and reviewers are organizational remedies outside the plugin.
entries.reason: The author reproduced the method's shape but not its social quality controls.

entries.note: Only the orchestrating session can dispatch sub-agents; this is Claude Code architecture.
entries.reason: Python in a plugin script cannot invoke Claude Code sub-agents; only the orchestrating session can.

entries.note: Agent dispatch being a conversation-model tool is platform design.
entries.reason: Claude Code's agent-dispatch tool is available only to the conversation model, not to shell commands.

entries.note: Scripts cannot emit model tool calls; platform fact.
entries.reason: Tools are dispatched through model tool calls, which scripts cannot emit.

entries.note: No Bash-exposed CLI subcommand for in-session agents is Claude Code's choice.
entries.reason: No CLI subcommand for spawning an in-session agent is exposed to Bash.

entries.note: Scripts as leaf tools returning text is Claude Code's architecture.
entries.reason: The architecture treats scripts as leaf tools returning text, not orchestrators.

entries.note: Headless claude invocations using separate sessions, cost and auth is platform behaviour.
entries.reason: Headless claude invocations start separate sessions with their own cost and auth.

entries.note: Plugin documentation lacking script-initiated model call patterns is outside plugin control.
entries.reason: Plugin documentation offers no pattern for script-initiated model calls.

entries.note: Extra reviewer agents are unnecessary; assemble's stdlib hygiene report supplies a global quality pass without dispatch.
entries.reason: Adding a model review step would require the orchestrating skill to dispatch extra reviewer agents.

entries.note: Orchestration load is reduced by plan grouping tasks into capped waves the skill dispatches in turn.
entries.reason: The skill workflow already coordinates 26 agents plus a fixed assemble step.

entries.note: hygiene.json needs no reviewer prompt template or new fragment format; assemble generates it directly.
entries.reason: A reviewer pass would need another prompt template and fragment format.

entries.note: Postponed script changes describe past sequencing; the review need is covered by IMP-06.
entries.reason: Extending the plan output with review tasks needs script changes the author postponed.

entries.note: Moving wave grouping into plan output keeps skill instructions short, lowering step-skipping risk.
entries.reason: Longer skill instructions increase the chance the orchestrator skips steps.

entries.note: Quality flags go to hygiene.json on disk, so no reviewer results flood the orchestrator context.
entries.reason: The orchestrator's context would fill further with reviewer results.

entries.note: Only cheap local checks belong in the fix loop; a model judge there is declined.
entries.reason: The check runs inside each sub-agent's fix loop, where only a cheap local call fits.

entries.note: Iterate-until-OK gets an explicit fix-loop cap with a FAILED reply carrying the first error.
entries.reason: Each sub-agent must iterate until OK, so the check must be fast and repeatable.

entries.note: Self-approval bias is sidestepped by independent mechanical hygiene flags computed at assembly.
entries.reason: A sub-agent judging its own output tends to approve it, reducing self-review value.

entries.note: Restricted nested agent spawning from sub-agents is a Claude Code limitation.
entries.reason: Nested agent spawning from within sub-agents is restricted or unavailable.

entries.note: Nuanced model feedback inside the blocking loop is declined; parse-error messages remain the loop's contract.
entries.reason: The loop was designed around parse errors with clear messages, not nuanced feedback.

entries.note: Agent instructions add targeted Edit repairs, so fixes need not rewrite whole subtrees.
entries.reason: Quality feedback would require rewriting whole subtrees, which the loop cannot express.

entries.note: The assembly-time hygiene report is the global pass detecting cross-branch duplicates.
entries.reason: Isolated branch agents cannot see sibling fragments, so cross-branch duplication checks need a global pass.

entries.note: Branch prompts gain the other level-1/level-2 reasons as causes covered elsewhere.
entries.reason: Parallel dispatch gives each agent only its ancestor chain, for speed.

entries.note: Waiting for sibling fragments would serialize the run; sequential feeding between branches is declined.
entries.reason: Sibling fragments are written concurrently and incomplete when a branch checks itself.

entries.note: Assembly stays deterministic Python but now also emits duplicate and restatement flags.
entries.reason: The only global step is assembly, which is Python and thus deterministic.

entries.note: Instead of sharing all fragments, prompts share only the cheap level-1/2 digest.
entries.reason: Sharing all fragments with a reviewer would require a very large context.

entries.note: Parallelism is kept while sibling-aware prompts add lightweight cross-branch coordination.
entries.reason: The design optimized parallelism over coordination between branches.

entries.note: The mechanics-versus-judgment split is kept and documented, naming which mechanical aids are allowed.
entries.reason: The script was designed as a pure data utility that separates mechanics from judgment.

entries.note: The scripts-deterministic, models-reason convention is retained rationale with nothing to change.
entries.reason: The author follows a convention of scripts for deterministic work and models for reasoning.

entries.note: Pure, deterministic functions are locked in by stdlib unittest coverage for plan, check and assemble.
entries.reason: Pure functions are easier to debug when fragment assembly fails.

entries.note: Model calls inside the utility stay declined, preserving clear failure responsibility.
entries.reason: Mixing model calls into the utility would blur responsibility for failures.

entries.note: Subcommand ordering before quality was considered is past sequence; hygiene now joins assemble via IMP-06.
entries.reason: The plan, check, and assemble subcommands were defined before quality validation was considered.

entries.note: The empty judgment slot is declared the user's, with mechanical aids filling what can be mechanized.
entries.reason: Clean separation looked architecturally correct even though it left the judgment slot empty.

entries.note: Avoiding a flaky model judge in validation is the catalog's declined LLM-judge disposition.
entries.reason: Model-based judging is nondeterministic, so the author avoided a check that could flake across runs.

entries.note: Endless fix loops from flaky verdicts are exactly why the blocking LLM judge is declined.
entries.reason: A flaky check would trap sub-agents in endless fix loops.

entries.note: True: why-expander says repeat until OK without a numeric cap; IMP-12 adds a fix-loop cap.
entries.reason: Sub-agents are instructed to repeat until OK with no retry cap.

entries.note: Shifting model-judge rejections are avoided by declining model judgment inside the fix loop.
entries.reason: A model judge may reject a revised reason for a different cause on each pass.

entries.note: Same-family self-preference in evaluators is a model behaviour fact.

entries.note: Position and ordering effects in pairwise judgments are model behaviour facts.

entries.note: Authoritative-looking but biased verdicts are avoided by keeping model judges out of validation.

entries.reason: Reproducible results were valued for comparing plugin versions and debugging.

entries.note: Unit tests pin identical check verdicts on fixed fragment fixtures.
entries.reason: Deterministic validation makes the same fragment always pass or fail identically.

entries.note: The eval suite grades shape validity and hygiene presence deterministically, supporting version comparisons.
entries.reason: Regression comparisons are meaningless if the grader itself varies run to run.

entries.note: Model version updates altering judge behaviour are outside plugin control.
entries.reason: Model version updates silently alter judge behavior over time.

entries.note: Developers trusting reproducible tools is general engineering psychology.
entries.reason: Developers trust tools more when rerunning gives the same answer.

entries.note: Claude Code exposes no seed or pinning control for sub-agent calls.

entries.reason: Tight thresholds cause mass rewrites while loose ones accept junk.

entries.note: Binary shape validity avoiding thresholds explains the past design; nothing further actionable.

entries.note: Viewing probabilistic evaluation as research is industry perception.

entries.note: Shared blind spots in self-evaluation are a model property outside plugin control.

entries.reason: No human-labeled examples existed to confirm whether a judge agreed with people.

entries.reason: A judge pass would add another large token cost on top of the ~150k-token output.

entries.reason: Judging 3,905 reasons requires reading the whole tree or dispatching many parallel chunks.

entries.reason: The fan-out already consumes 26 sub-agent calls, making extra passes feel excessive.

entries.reason: Cost per run was never measured, so judge overhead could not be weighed concretely.

entries.reason: Users on metered plans were assumed to balk at roughly doubled spending.

entries.reason: Cheaper model selection for a judge role was not wired into the agent definitions.

entries.reason: Judge verdicts are non-deterministic, clashing with a script that returns crisp OK or errors.

entries.reason: The check contract is binary, leaving no place for scored or probabilistic results.

entries.reason: Agents loop until OK, so a flaky judge could trigger endless retry cycles.

entries.reason: No retry cap or tolerance setting exists to absorb inconsistent verdicts.

entries.reason: A Python validator cannot call a model without adding credentials and dependencies.

entries.note: Reproducibility remains valued; hygiene flags (IMP-06) are deterministic, so nothing further needed.
entries.reason: Reproducibility was prized so the same fragment always validates the same way.

entries.note: Agent instructions gain concrete specificity criteria and a specific-vs-generic example as a working standard.
entries.reason: No rubric existed defining what makes a reason good enough to pass.

entries.note: Optional context intake supplies problem-specific details that ground plausibility.
entries.reason: Causal plausibility is hard to specify without domain knowledge of each user's problem.

entries.reason: The agent instructions list style rules but no measurable acceptance criteria.

entries.reason: Nobody collected sample good and bad reasons from which to derive a rubric.

entries.note: State of Five Whys literature is outside the plugin's control.
entries.reason: Five Whys literature offers heuristics, not scoring standards, for cause quality.

entries.reason: Rubric drafting was deferred until a full real run revealed actual failure modes.

entries.reason: The user was positioned as sole judge of which causes matter in their context.

entries.reason: A filtered tree would hide what was removed, reducing transparency to the user.

entries.reason: No flag-without-delete option was considered, so judgment implied silent removal.

entries.note: Author's prior tooling experiences explain distrust; flags-only design (IMP-06) respects it.

entries.note: A full 3,905-reason real run completed on 2026-09-13, providing failure data.
entries.reason: No failure data existed because a full 3,905-reason run was never executed.

entries.note: Outline-before-write and grounding instructions address attention across long outputs.
entries.reason: Prominent placement of rules was assumed to hold attention across very long outputs.

entries.note: Branch prompts will list other level-1/level-2 reasons as causes covered elsewhere.
